canonical_statement: The study sought to characterize the incidence, causes, timing, and outcomes of 90-day readmissions after chronic or subacute subdural hematoma hospitalization and to identify patient phenotypes with distinct readmission-risk profiles using machine-learning-driven clustering.
The investigators performed a retrospective cohort study using the Nationwide Readmissions Database from 2016 through 2022.
The Nationwide Readmissions Database uses verified patient linkage numbers to track readmissions within the same state and calendar year.

Eligible patients were adults aged 18 years or older with a nonelective hospitalization carrying a primary diagnosis of subdural hematoma and coding consistent with chronic, subacute, or acute-on-chronic disease.

population.label: Adults aged >=18 years with nonelective SDH hospitalization and chronic/subacute/acute-on-chronic coding
inclusion_criteria: Primary diagnosis of SDH with specified chronic/subacute coding

canonical_statement: Patients who died during the index admission, had do-not-resuscitate orders, were nonresidents, or had missing key data fields were excluded.
Patients discharged in October through December were excluded to ensure complete 90-day follow-up within the calendar year.

population.label: Qualifying cSDH/sSDH admissions
exclusion_criteria: Index discharge in October, November, or December

canonical_statement: Patients who underwent middle meningeal artery embolization during the index admission or whose first readmission was an elective middle meningeal artery embolization procedure were excluded.
The primary outcome was the first all-cause hospital readmission within 90 days of index discharge.

Readmission reasons were assigned hierarchically to 7 mutually exclusive categories: surgical SDH, nonsurgical SDH or seizure, stroke or venous thromboembolism, cardiovascular, infection, other, or not readmitted.
Functional decline was defined as worsening discharge disposition from the index admission to readmission across an ordered scale from routine home discharge through death.

outcome.definition: Worsening discharge disposition from index admission to readmission

canonical_statement: New disability was defined among patients initially discharged home with routine self-care as requiring additional services on readmission or dying.

outcome.definition: Among routine index discharges, readmission requiring additional services or resulting in death

canonical_statement: Inability to return home was defined among patients discharged to any home setting after the index admission as discharge to a facility or death after readmission.

concept.text: Unable to return home after readmission

outcome.definition: Among patients discharged home after index admission, facility discharge or death after readmission

canonical_statement: Readmission costs were inflation-adjusted to 2022 US dollars using the Consumer Price Index and converted from charges using hospital-specific cost-to-charge ratios.
The first stage of the phenotyping pipeline trained a multinomial LightGBM gradient-boosted decision-tree model to predict the 7-class readmission outcome.
The LightGBM model used index-admission demographics, comorbidity indices, SDH subtype, surgery type, procedure complexity, diagnosis and CCSR features, and hospital characteristics.
Model training used 5-fold stratified cross-validation, Bayesian hyperparameter optimization over 100 iterations, and post hoc temperature scaling for probability calibration.
The LightGBM model was used as a feature-transformation tool rather than as a clinical prediction instrument.
SHAP values were calculated across all 7 readmission classes for the 50 most important features, creating a 350-dimensional patient-level matrix of readmission-risk attribution profiles.
K-means clustering was applied to the 350-dimensional SHAP matrix to identify patient phenotypes.

The number of clusters was selected using the elbow method, Bayesian Information Criterion, mean silhouette width, consensus-clustering stability across 100 bootstrap resamples, and pathophysiologic congruency of cluster characteristics.

The authors selected K-means because SHAP values share an additive log-odds scale and argued that alternative full-covariance Gaussian-mixture and hierarchical approaches were impractical or ill-conditioned at the study dimensionality and sample size.

Baseline and cluster comparisons used Kruskal-Wallis tests for continuous variables and chi-square tests for categorical variables; cluster-by-readmission observed-to-expected ratios used exact Poisson 95% confidence intervals.
The Nationwide Readmissions Database data used in the study are publicly available for purchase from the Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project.
The final cohort contained 22,387 patients; mean age was 70.8 years, 29.6% were female, and 58.9% underwent surgery during the index hospitalization.

canonical_statement: Cluster 1: low acuity contained 8,913 patients (39.8%). The largest cluster was labeled low acuity and was characterized by more routine discharge, no atrial fibrillation, shorter length of stay, low dementia prevalence, and low Elixhauser comorbidity.

Cluster 2: elderly/frail contained 3,725 patients (16.6%). The elderly/frail cluster was characterized by facility discharge, older age, high dementia prevalence, other CNS disorders, and elevated CHA2DS2-VASc scores.

Cluster 3: atrial fibrillation contained 3,794 patients (16.9%). The atrial fibrillation cluster had near-universal atrial fibrillation and cardiac dysrhythmias and higher HAS-BLED and CHA2DS2-VASc scores.
Cluster 4: young/healthy contained 3,247 patients (14.5%). The young/healthy cluster had the youngest age and the lowest cardiac disease and comorbidity burden across the reported indices.

Cluster 5: high acuity contained 2,708 patients (12.1%). The high-acuity cluster had the longest hospital stays, the greatest non-CNS procedure burden, the most diagnoses, more encephalopathy, and higher comorbidity counts.
Cluster 1: low acuity had an observed-to-expected ratio of 1.29 (95% CI 1.19-1.38) for surgical sdh readmission.
Cluster 2: elderly/frail had an observed-to-expected ratio of 1.71 (95% CI 1.51-1.92) for infection readmission.
Cluster 3: atrial fibrillation had an observed-to-expected ratio of 1.91 (95% CI 1.52-2.29) for stroke/vte readmission.
Cluster 3: atrial fibrillation had an observed-to-expected ratio of 2.43 (95% CI 2.08-2.80) for cardiovascular readmission.
Cluster 4: young/healthy had an observed-to-expected ratio of 0.05 (95% CI 0.00-0.12) for cardiovascular readmission.
Cluster 5: high acuity had an observed-to-expected ratio of 1.80 (95% CI 1.55-2.05) for infection readmission.
Cluster 5: high acuity had an observed-to-expected ratio of 1.46 (95% CI 1.31-1.61) for other-cause readmission.
The authors concluded that surgical SDH recurrence represents only about one in five readmissions and that fewer than half of 90-day readmissions are directly SDH-related.

The authors concluded that nonsurgical and non-SDH readmissions can carry morbidity and mortality equal to or worse than surgical recurrence and argued for postdischarge care and trial endpoints that extend beyond reoperation.
The authors stated that the identified phenotypes are hypothesis-generating and that more comprehensive care models and inclusive clinical trial designs are needed.

The Nationwide Readmissions Database is an administrative claims database and lacks imaging findings, laboratory values, medication doses, outpatient records, and other clinical granularity that could improve discrimination and phenotyping.
Postdischarge deaths occurring without a hospital readmission are not captured in the Nationwide Readmissions Database, so such deaths may be misclassified within the non-readmission outcome.
Excluding middle meningeal artery embolization patients, patients with do-not-resuscitate status, and late-calendar-year discharges may have introduced selection bias and limited generalizability.
The database lacked race/ethnicity, area deprivation index, and other socioeconomic variables beyond rurality and median household income of residence.
The multinomial model achieved only modest overall discrimination for specific readmission reason, with an AUC of approximately 0.66.
The machine-learning clustering analysis was exploratory and hypothesis-generating, and the identified phenotypes require prospective and independent external validation.
